name: Acetyl tetrapeptide-3

card.summary: A hair-anchoring cosmetic peptide (found in Capixyl) tested only inside a multi-herbal combination against 3% minoxidil in one small trial.
card.note: The only listed trial tested a combination product, in 32 people.

quick.overview:
Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is a cosmetic peptide used in hair-density topicals and is named as the hair-anchoring ingredient in Capixyl. It is usually combined with plant extracts.

One 24-week randomized, triple-blind trial in 32 people compared a combination of biochanin A, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 and ginseng extracts with 3% minoxidil solution in androgenetic alopecia, so the peptide's own effect was not isolated.
quick.mechanism: Mechanistic claims are made by product makers; the studies reviewed here evaluated outcomes of the combination rather than the peptide's mechanism.
quick.risks: The trial assessed a safety profile for the combination as a stated objective [1]. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than an approved hair-loss drug.

lead: Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is a synthetic cosmetic peptide used in topical products for thinning hair, most often as part of the ingredient blend Capixyl, where it appears together with biochanin A and plant extracts such as ginseng [1][3]. People use these topicals to make the scalp look fuller, aiming for denser-looking hair at the crown and temples.

A 24-week, randomized, triple-blind controlled trial in 32 men and women with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia compared a combination of biochanin A, acetyl tetrapeptide-3 and ginseng extracts with 3% minoxidil solution. Terminal hair count rose 8.3 percent with the combination and 8.7 percent with minoxidil, with no statistically significant difference between groups; only the minoxidil group had an adverse reaction, one case of scalp eczema [1][3]. Because the product combined three ingredients, the result cannot be attributed to the peptide alone.

A 2026 systematic review in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology screened 981 records and included 14 clinical studies of peptides for hair loss; it graded acetyl tetrapeptide-3 among the peptides with a Grade B recommendation and concluded that peptide combinations, particularly those containing it, were effective and well-tolerated alternatives to conventional therapies [2][3]. A 2025 review of 24 articles and technical files on topical alternatives, which covered Capixyl, noted small samples, few comparisons with standard therapy and conflicts of interest [3].

chain: Peptide-containing topical is applied to the scalp
Product makers say it supports the hair anchoring and growth environment
angle.text: The ingredient is used in cosmetic scalp products that aim to thicken the look of thinning hair. In the one randomized trial, a combination containing it produced terminal hair count gains similar to 3% minoxidil over 24 weeks.

paras: Acetyl tetrapeptide-3 is formulated into serums and lotions for hair thinning, usually with biochanin A and other plant extracts under the brand name Capixyl [1][3]. Product makers describe the combination as supporting hair anchoring and the follicle environment; the studies evaluated outcomes of the combination rather than isolating the peptide's mechanism [1][3].

The 24-week trial by Lueangarun and Panchaprateep (Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology, 2020) randomized 32 participants with mild to moderate androgenetic alopecia to twice-daily 1 mL applications of the herbal combination or 3% minoxidil. Terminal hair count increased 8.3 percent and 8.7 percent respectively, with no significant difference, and the authors recommended larger, longer studies [1][3].

The 2026 systematic review by Joerg, Zafar and Jagdeo identified 14 eligible studies of peptide-containing therapies, graded acetyl tetrapeptide-3 as Grade B alongside biotinoyl tripeptide-1, glycyl-histidyl-lysine and Gly-Pro-Ile-Gly-Ser, and graded QR678 products Grade C [2][3].

A 2025 International Journal of Trichology review described Capixyl among topical hair-growth actives that were mostly tested as combination formulations, and suggested such products may serve as add-on or alternative options for people who cannot tolerate standard treatments [3].
In the 24-week trial, the only adverse reaction was one case of scalp eczema in the minoxidil group [3]. It is a cosmetic ingredient rather than an approved hair-loss drug.

timeline.event: 24-week randomized trial of a combination containing acetyl tetrapeptide-3 versus 3% minoxidil published [1].
Review of topical alternatives for hair loss, including Capixyl, published in the International Journal of Trichology [3].
Systematic review of peptides for hair loss published [2].
